claims.evidence: This is supported by live imaging and cytological data showing chromosome separation before metaphase in the absence of spindles.

claims.claim: Both reduplication responses require the spindle assembly checkpoint protein Mad2.
claims.source: Both reduplication responses require the spindle assembly checkpoint protein Mad2.
claims.evidence: This is supported by genetic experiments showing mad2 mutant phenotypes in both contexts.

claims.claim: Mad2 delays anaphase separation of metaphase polytene chromosomes.
claims.source: While Mad2 delays anaphase separation of metaphase polytene chromosomes, Mad2's control of overall mitotic timing ensures efficient SIRS.
claims.evidence: This is supported by live imaging data showing extended metaphase in wild-type vs mad2 mutants with diplochromosomes.

claims.claim: Mad2's control of overall mitotic timing ensures efficient SIRS.
claims.source: While Mad2 delays anaphase separation of metaphase polytene chromosomes, Mad2's control of overall mitotic timing ensures efficient SIRS.
claims.evidence: This is supported by data showing incomplete SIRS and DNA bridges in mad2 mutants due to shortened mitotic timing.

claims.claim: During mitosis, chromatids associate in sister pairs, which facilitates their bi-orientation and subsequent segregation to opposite spindle poles.
claims.source: During mitosis, chromatids associate in sister pairs, which facilitates their bi-orientation and subsequent segregation to opposite spindle poles.
claims.evidence: This is established knowledge about normal mitotic chromosome behavior.

claims.claim: Following a single extra S-phase, cells frequently form diplochromosomes: four sister chromatids conjoined at centromeres.
claims.source: Following a single extra S-phase, cells frequently form diplochromosomes: four sister chromatids conjoined at centromeres (White, 1935).
claims.evidence: This is supported by a citation to White, 1935 and by experimental data in the manuscript.

claims.claim: Multiple layers of physical connections tightly intertwine the multiple sister chromatids of polytene chromosomes.
claims.source: While incompletely understood, it is appreciated that multiple layers of physical connections tightly intertwine the multiple sister chromatids of polytene chromosomes.
claims.evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature.

claims.claim: Physical connections in polytene chromosomes likely include cohesins.
claims.source: These connections likely include cohesins (Cunningham et al., 2012; Pauli et al., 2010) as well as topological entanglements that can be removed by Condensin II activity (Bauer et al., 2012; Smith et al., 2013; Wallace et al., 2015).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citations to Cunningham et al., 2012 and Pauli et al., 2010.

claims.claim: Physical connections in polytene chromosomes include topological entanglements that can be removed by Condensin II activity.
claims.source: These connections likely include cohesins (Cunningham et al., 2012; Pauli et al., 2010) as well as topological entanglements that can be removed by Condensin II activity (Bauer et al., 2012; Smith et al., 2013; Wallace et al., 2015).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citations to Bauer et al., 2012; Smith et al., 2013; Wallace et al., 2015.

claims.claim: Recurring regions of DNA under-replication occur between chromatids in some polytene cells.
claims.source: Additionally, recurring regions of DNA under-replication occur between chromatids in some polytene cells (Beliaeva et al., 1998; Gall et al., 1971; Hannibal et al., 2014; Nordman et al., 2011; Yarosh and Spradling, 2014) whereas DNA replication is more complete in others (Dej and Spradling, 1999; Fox et al., 2010).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citations to multiple studies.

claims.claim: DNA replication is more complete in some polytene cells compared to others.
claims.source: Additionally, recurring regions of DNA under-replication occur between chromatids in some polytene cells (Beliaeva et al., 1998; Gall et al., 1971; Hannibal et al., 2014; Nordman et al., 2011; Yarosh and Spradling, 2014) whereas DNA replication is more complete in others (Dej and Spradling, 1999; Fox et al., 2010).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citations to Dej and Spradling, 1999 and Fox et al., 2010.

claims.claim: Pairing between homologs occurs in some polytene cells.
claims.source: In addition to connections between sister chromatids, another layer of chromosome association - pairing between homologs - also occurs in some polytene cells.
claims.evidence: This is supported by citations and experimental observations in the manuscript.

claims.claim: Homolog pairing in polytene cells results in polyploid/polytene cells that exhibit only the haploid number of distinct chromosomes.
claims.source: This pairing results in polyploid/polytene cells that exhibit only the haploid number of distinct chromosomes (Metz, 1916; White, 1954).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citations to Metz, 1916 and White, 1954, and by experimental data in the manuscript.

claims.claim: Mitosis in polytene cells is considered 'ill-advised for mechanical reasons'.
claims.source: Given these multiple physical connections between polytene chromatids, mitosis in polytene cells is considered 'ill-advised for mechanical reasons' (Edgar and Orr-Weaver, 2001).
claims.evidence: This is a quote from Edgar and Orr-Weaver, 2001.

claims.claim: Separation of polytene diplochromosomes at anaphase causes chromosome mis-segregation.
claims.source: Indeed, separation of polytene diplochromosomes at anaphase causes chromosome mis-segregation (Vidwans et al., 2002).
claims.evidence: This is supported by a citation to Vidwans et al., 2002.

claims.claim: Polytene chromosomes have been observed in cells from spontaneous human abortions.
claims.source: Polytene chromosomes have been observed in cells from spontaneous human abortions (Therman et al., 1978), in muscular dystrophy patients (Schmidt et al., 2011), in a variety of tumors (Biesele and Poyner, 1943; Erenpreisa et al., 2009; Therman et al., 1983) and can also precede tumor formation in mice (Davoli and de Lange, 2012).
claims.evidence: This is supported by a citation to Therman et al., 1978.

claims.claim: Polytene chromosomes have been observed in muscular dystrophy patients.
claims.source: Polytene chromosomes have been observed in cells from spontaneous human abortions (Therman et al., 1978), in muscular dystrophy patients (Schmidt et al., 2011), in a variety of tumors (Biesele and Poyner, 1943; Erenpreisa et al., 2009; Therman et al., 1983) and can also precede tumor formation in mice (Davoli and de Lange, 2012).
claims.evidence: This is supported by a citation to Schmidt et al., 2011.

claims.claim: Polytene chromosomes have been observed in a variety of tumors.
claims.source: Polytene chromosomes have been observed in cells from spontaneous human abortions (Therman et al., 1978), in muscular dystrophy patients (Schmidt et al., 2011), in a variety of tumors (Biesele and Poyner, 1943; Erenpreisa et al., 2009; Therman et al., 1983) and can also precede tumor formation in mice (Davoli and de Lange, 2012).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citations to Biesele and Poyner, 1943; Erenpreisa et al., 2009; Therman et al., 1983.

claims.claim: Polytene chromosomes can precede tumor formation in mice.
claims.source: Polytene chromosomes have been observed in cells from spontaneous human abortions (Therman et al., 1978), in muscular dystrophy patients (Schmidt et al., 2011), in a variety of tumors (Biesele and Poyner, 1943; Erenpreisa et al., 2009; Therman et al., 1983) and can also precede tumor formation in mice (Davoli and de Lange, 2012).
claims.evidence: This is supported by a citation to Davoli and de Lange, 2012.

claims.claim: Polytene chromosomes occur after treatment with Topoisomerase II inhibitors.
claims.source: Polytene chromosomes also occur after treatment with currently used anti-mitotic chemotherapeutics such as those that inhibit Topoisomerase II (Cantero et al., 2006; Sumner, 1998).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citations to Cantero et al., 2006 and Sumner, 1998.

claims.claim: Disruption of spindle formation causes genome reduplication and polyteny.
claims.source: Disruption of numerous other processes crucial for mitosis, including spindle formation (Goyanes and Schvartzman, 1981; Takanari et al., 1985) sister chromatid cohesion (Wirth et al., 2006) or genome integrity control (Davoli et al., 2010) also cause genome reduplication and polyteny.
claims.evidence: This is supported by citations to Goyanes and Schvartzman, 1981 and Takanari et al., 1985.

claims.claim: Disruption of sister chromatid cohesion causes genome reduplication and polyteny.
claims.source: Disruption of numerous other processes crucial for mitosis, including spindle formation (Goyanes and Schvartzman, 1981; Takanari et al., 1985) sister chromatid cohesion (Wirth et al., 2006) or genome integrity control (Davoli et al., 2010) also cause genome reduplication and polyteny.
claims.evidence: This is supported by a citation to Wirth et al., 2006.

claims.claim: Disruption of genome integrity control causes genome reduplication and polyteny.
claims.source: Disruption of numerous other processes crucial for mitosis, including spindle formation (Goyanes and Schvartzman, 1981; Takanari et al., 1985) sister chromatid cohesion (Wirth et al., 2006) or genome integrity control (Davoli et al., 2010) also cause genome reduplication and polyteny.
claims.evidence: This is supported by a citation to Davoli et al., 2010.

claims.claim: Programmed genome reduplication cycles produce polytene chromosomes in many plant, insect, and mammalian species, including humans.
claims.source: Programmed genome reduplication cycles of successive S-phase without M-phase (endocycles, Edgar et al., 2014; Fox and Duronio, 2013 see nomenclature) produce polytene chromosomes in many plant, insect, and mammalian species, including humans (Zhimulev et al., 2004; Zybina et al., 1996).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citations to Edgar et al., 2014; Fox and Duronio, 2013; Zhimulev et al., 2004; Zybina et al., 1996.

claims.claim: Rectal papillar cells in Drosophila hindgut are built entirely by mitosis of endocycled cells.
claims.source: In contrast, we previously demonstrated that rectal papilla (hereafter: papillar cells), ion-absorbing structures in the Drosophila hindgut, are built entirely by mitosis of endocycled cells (Fox et al., 2010; Schoenfelder et al., 2014).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citations to Fox et al., 2010 and Schoenfelder et al., 2014.

claims.claim: Polytene chromosomes were never observed in hundreds of papillar metaphases.
claims.source: Surprisingly, we never observed polytene chromosomes in hundreds of papillar metaphases (Fox et al., 2010; Schoenfelder et al., 2014), suggesting papillar cells are programmed to either avoid or eliminate polyteny and its associated mitotic defects.
claims.evidence: This is supported by citations to Fox et al., 2010 and Schoenfelder et al., 2014.

claims.claim: Previous studies suggest that polyteny can be at least partially undone without anaphase in both normal and tumorous tissue.
claims.source: Interestingly, previous studies suggest that polyteny can be at least partially undone without anaphase in both normal and tumorous tissue (Dej and Spradling, 1999; Grell, 1946; Levan and Hauschka, 1953).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citations to Dej and Spradling, 1999; Grell, 1946; Levan and Hauschka, 1953.

claims.claim: Mad2 inhibits the Anaphase Promoting Complex to delay anaphase in response to unattached or tensionless kinetochores.
claims.source: Both reduplication responses require the conserved spindle assembly checkpoint (SAC) protein Mad2, which inhibits the Anaphase Promoting Complex to both delay anaphase in response to unattached or tensionless kinetochores and to also regulate overall mitotic timing from nuclear envelope breakdown (NEBD) to anaphase onset (London and Biggins, 2014; Musacchio, 2015).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citations to London and Biggins, 2014 and Musacchio, 2015.

claims.claim: Mad2 regulates overall mitotic timing from nuclear envelope breakdown (NEBD) to anaphase onset.
claims.source: Both reduplication responses require the conserved spindle assembly checkpoint (SAC) protein Mad2, which inhibits the Anaphase Promoting Complex to both delay anaphase in response to unattached or tensionless kinetochores and to also regulate overall mitotic timing from nuclear envelope breakdown (NEBD) to anaphase onset (London and Biggins, 2014; Musacchio, 2015).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citations to London and Biggins, 2014 and Musacchio, 2015.

claims.claim: In reduplicated cells that retain polytene chromosomes at metaphase, Mad2 is involved in a SAC wait-anaphase response.
claims.source: In reduplicated cells that retain polytene chromosomes at metaphase, we show Mad2 is involved in a SAC wait-anaphase response.
claims.evidence: This is supported by experimental data showing Mad2-dependent metaphase extension in cells with diplochromosomes.

claims.claim: The anaphase delay in cells with metaphase polytene chromosomes does not fully prevent mitotic errors and resulting aneuploidy.
claims.source: This anaphase delay does not fully prevent the mitotic errors and the resulting aneuploidy associated with mitosis of polytene chromosomes, but it substantially reduces apoptosis, tissue malformation, and organismal death.
claims.evidence: This is supported by experimental data showing lagging chromosomes and aneuploidy even with Mad2 present, but increased apoptosis and lethality in mad2 mutants.

claims.claim: The anaphase delay substantially reduces apoptosis, tissue malformation, and organismal death in cells with metaphase polytene chromosomes.
claims.source: This anaphase delay does not fully prevent the mitotic errors and the resulting aneuploidy associated with mitosis of polytene chromosomes, but it substantially reduces apoptosis, tissue malformation, and organismal death.
claims.evidence: This is supported by experimental data comparing survival and apoptosis in HS>fzr vs HS>fzr, mad2 animals.

claims.claim: Polytene chromosomes undergo a dynamic, spindle-independent process termed Separation-Into-Recent-Sisters (SIRS).
claims.source: In this response, polytene chromosomes undergo a dynamic, spindle-independent process we term Separation Into Recent Sister chromatid pairs (SIRS), which eliminates any trace of polyteny before anaphase.
claims.evidence: This is supported by live imaging data showing chromosome separation in the presence of colcemid.

claims.claim: SIRS eliminates any trace of polyteny before anaphase.
claims.source: In this response, polytene chromosomes undergo a dynamic, spindle-independent process we term Separation Into Recent Sister chromatid pairs (SIRS), which eliminates any trace of polyteny before anaphase.
claims.evidence: This is supported by cytological and live imaging data showing separated chromosomes at metaphase after SIRS.

claims.claim: Mitosis with metaphase polytene chromosomes does not trigger a Mad2-dependent anaphase delay during SIRS.
claims.source: Unlike mitosis with metaphase polytene chromosomes, mitosis with SIRS does not trigger a Mad2-dependent anaphase delay.
claims.evidence: This is supported by data showing no difference in metaphase length between first and second papillar divisions.

claims.claim: Mad2 promotes efficient SIRS by allowing sufficient time between nuclear envelope breakdown and anaphase.
claims.source: Yet, we find Mad2 promotes efficient SIRS by allowing sufficient time between nuclear envelope breakdown and anaphase, which allows polytene chromosomes to separate into conventional mitotic sister chromatid pairs.
claims.evidence: This is supported by data showing incomplete SIRS and DNA bridges in mad2 mutants with shortened NEBD-to-anaphase timing.

claims.claim: fzr overexpression transforms mitotic cycles into endocycles.
claims.source: fzr overexpression was previously shown to transform mitotic cycles into endocycles (Sigrist and Lehner, 1997).
claims.evidence: This is supported by a citation to Sigrist and Lehner, 1997.

claims.claim: Pulsed fzr overexpression temporarily eliminates expression of the S/G2/M mRFP-CyclinB reporter in wing imaginal disc cells.
claims.source: Using the cell cycle marker system Fly-FUCCI (Zielke et al., 2014; Figure 1B) we find that pulsed fzr overexpression temporarily eliminates expression of the S/G2/M mRFP-CyclinB reporter in wing imaginal disc cells (Figure 1C vs. C', D).
claims.evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1C, C', and D.

claims.claim: Pulsed fzr expression promotes G1 accumulation (91% of cells compared to 36% in controls).
claims.source: Together, these data suggest HS>fzr promotes G1 accumulation (91% of cells compared to 36% in controls, Figure 1B–D).
claims.evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1B-D.

claims.claim: For up to 7 hr after fzr overexpression, there is essentially no mitosis in the wing imaginal disc.
claims.source: For up to 7 hr after fzr overexpression, there is essentially no mitosis in the wing imaginal disc, whereas wing cells in heat shocked wild type flies continue to divide after heat shock (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A,B).
claims.evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1A,B.

claims.claim: Pulsed fzr expression converts G2 cells to a G1 state by eliminating mitotic cyclins.
claims.source: Based on previous studies of fzr function and our FUCCI and Phospho-Histone H3 data, we conclude that pulsed fzr expression converts G2 cells to a G1 state by eliminating mitotic cyclins (Figure 1A).
claims.evidence: This is based on inference from prior studies and experimental data.

claims.claim: Ten hours after heat shock, 41% of mitotic HS>fzr cells are tetraploid.
claims.source: At this time-point, we observe frequent tetraploidy (41% of mitotic cells, equivalent to 93% of all G2 cells prior to heat shock, Figure 1E v. F,F',H).
claims.evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1E, F, F', H.

claims.claim: When HS>fzr-induced tetraploid DNA first condenses post-heat shock, all chromatids of each chromosome type are closely aligned in a polytene configuration.
claims.source: When HS>fzr-induced tetraploid DNA first condenses post-heat shock, all chromatids of each chromosome type are closely aligned in a polytene configuration, as evidenced by having the haploid number of distinguishable chromosomes (four in females, Figure 1F).
claims.evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1F.

claims.claim: At the first metaphase after HS>fzr, 96% of tetraploid cells have diplochromosomes.
claims.source: Later, at the first metaphase, homologous chromosomes of each polytene are now completely separated, but the four centromeres of each group of sister chromatids remain conjoined within diplochromosomes (observed for 96% of tetraploid cells, Figure 1F' inset, H).
claims.evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1F' inset and H.

claims.claim: Following the division of cells with diplochromosomes, 8.6% of mitotic cells are tetraploid-aneuploid with one or two extra or missing chromosomes.
claims.source: Following the division of cells with diplochromosomes, we observe tetraploid-aneuploid cells with one or two extra or missing chromosomes (8.6% of mitotic cells).
claims.evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1G, H.

claims.claim: Control diploid cells divide without errors.
claims.source: Control diploid cells divide without errors (Figure 1I No HS, J, Video 1).
claims.evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1I, J and Video 1.

claims.claim: 80% of tetraploid divisions with diplochromosomes exhibit lagging chromosomes, DNA bridges, or both.
claims.source: In contrast, most (80%) tetraploid divisions with diplochromosomes exhibit lagging chromosomes, DNA bridges, or both (Figure 1I HS+10 hr, J, Video 2).
claims.evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1I, J and Video 2.

claims.claim: Four chromatids of a diplochromosome quartet can segregate 3:1.
claims.source: In some of these divisions we clearly observe four chromatids of a diplochromosome quartet segregating 3:1 (in agreement with prior work in embryos by Vidwans et al., 2002, suggesting incomplete or imprecise sister chromatid disjunction is the cause of chromosome gains and losses (Figure 1I, Figure 1—figure supplement 1D, Video 2).
claims.evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1I, Figure 1—figure supplement 1D, and Video 2, and by citation to Vidwans et al., 2002.

claims.claim: Tetraploid cells in subsequent divisions (which lack diplochromosomes) have a substantially reduced error rate compared to cells with diplochromosomes.
claims.source: Mitotic errors in the first division of HS>fzr cells appear to result primarily from diplochromosomes and not tetraploidy itself, as tetraploid cells in the subsequent divisions (which lack diplochromosomes) do not exhibit obvious chromosome quartets and have a substantially reduced error rate (Figure 1J 4N, Figure 1—figure supplement 1E, Video 3).
claims.evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1J, Figure 1—figure supplement 1E, and Video 3.

claims.claim: Centrosome amplification does not appear to be a major contributor to mitotic errors in the first polyploid division of HS>fzr animals.
claims.source: However, centrosome amplification does not appear to be a major contributor to mitotic errors in the first (or subsequent) polyploid division of HS>fzr animals, as few tetraploid cells amplify centrosomes, and multipolar division is very rare (Figure 1—figure supplement 1F,G, Video 4).
claims.evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1F, G and Video 4.

claims.claim: Tetraploid-aneuploid cell divisions continue to occur for at least 5 days after genome reduplication.
claims.source: In spite of the high initial error rate caused by separation of diplochromosomes, tetraploid-aneuploid cell divisions continue to occur for at least 5 days after genome reduplication, as determined by cytology (Figure 1H HS+120 hr).
claims.evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1H.

claims.claim: Survival is only subtly affected in animals with mild (23.0% tetraploid [S.E.M. 4.9%]) levels of induced error-prone tetraploid progenitor division.
claims.source: Survival is only subtly affected in animals with mild (23.0% tetraploid [S.E.M. 4.9%]) levels of induced error-prone tetraploid progenitor division (Figure 2A), and resulting adult tissues appear normal (Figure 2B).
claims.evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2A and 2B.

claims.claim: When tetraploidy is increased by increasing the duration of heat shock, organism survival decreases in a tetraploid-dependent fashion.
claims.source: In contrast, when tetraploidy is further increased by increasing the duration of heat shock, organism survival decreases in a tetraploid-dependent fashion (Figure 2A, Figure 2—figure supplement 1A).
claims.evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2A and Figure 2—figure supplement 1A.

claims.claim: Metaphase in cells with diplochromosomes is significantly longer than in diploid cells.
claims.source: Metaphase in cells with diplochromosomes (Figure 2C, yellow dotted outline) is significantly longer than in diploid cells (Figure 2C blue dashed outline, Video 5, Figure 2D), consistent with previous work on diplochromosomes formed in Drosophila Securin mutants (Pandey et al., 2005).
claims.evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2C, D and Video 5, and by citation to Pandey et al., 2005.

claims.claim: Loss of mad2 eliminates the lengthened period of metaphase caused by diplochromosomes.
claims.source: To test this model, we examined SAC-defective mad2 null animals (Buffin et al., 2007; Emre et al., 2011) Figure 2—figure supplement 1B). Using live imaging of wing imaginal discs before and after heat shock, we find that loss of mad2 eliminates the lengthened period of metaphase caused by diplochromosomes (Figure 2D).
claims.evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2D and Figure 2—figure supplement 1B, and by citations to Buffin et al., 2007 and Emre et al., 2011.

claims.claim: BubR1-GFP is clearly evident on kinetochores following nuclear envelope break down in diploid cells and remains there until anaphase.
claims.source: We find that in diploid cells BubR1-GFP is clearly evident on kinetochores following nuclear envelope break down and remains there until anaphase. This signal is relatively evenly spread across all the kinetochores (Figure 2—figure supplement 1C, diploid, Video 6).
claims.evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1C and Video 6.

claims.claim: BubR1-GFP remains localized for much longer in cells with diplochromosomes and is often localized strongly to a specific kinetochore group rather than evenly distributed.
claims.source: In contrast BubR1-GFP remains localized for much longer in cells with diplochromosomes and is often localized strongly to a specific kinetochore group rather than evenly distributed, suggesting that a subset of diplochromosomes may have trouble forming attachments that satisfy the checkpoint (Figure 2—figure supplement 1C, diplochromosomes, Video 7)
claims.evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1C and Video 7.

claims.claim: mad2 null animals are viable with no obvious tissue defects.
claims.source: Although important for mitosis in cultured Drosophila S2 cells (Orr et al., 2007), the Mad2-directed SAC is reported to be dispensable in Drosophila tissue mitosis (Buffin et al., 2007; Emre et al., 2011). mad2 null animals are viable with no obvious tissue defects (Figure 2B; Buffin et al., 2007) due in part to an apoptotic response (Morais da Silva et al., 2013).
claims.evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2B and by citations to Buffin et al., 2007 and Morais da Silva et al., 2013.

claims.claim: Even at low levels of tetraploidy, few HS>fzr, mad2 animals survive to adulthood (15.4%).
claims.source: In contrast, the Mad2-dependent wait-anaphase response is essential during development of HS>fzr animals. Even at low levels of tetraploidy, which affect the survival of HS>fzr animals only slightly, few HS>fzr, mad2 animals survive to adulthood (15.4%, Figure 2A, Figure 2—figure supplement 1A).
claims.evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2A and Figure 2—figure supplement 1A.

claims.claim: HS>fzr, mad2 animals that survive have a variety of developmental defects in normally diploid tissues, including smaller eyes, ectopic wing veins, and melanotic abdominal masses.
claims.source: To understand why HS>fzr, mad2 animals have survival defects, we analyzed the surviving animals. In these animals, we find a variety of developmental defects in normally diploid tissues, including smaller eyes, ectopic wing veins, and melanotic abdominal masses (Figure 2B).
claims.evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2B.

claims.claim: Progenitor tissue from HS>fzr, mad2 animals have much higher rates of apoptotic cell death as shown by both TUNEL labeling and cleaved caspase staining.
claims.source: Increased apoptosis is associated with these tissue malformation phenotypes, as progenitor tissue from HS>fzr, mad2 animals have much higher rates of apoptotic cell death as shown by both TUNEL labeling (Figure 2E,F), and cleaved caspase staining (Figure 2—figure supplement 1D,E).
claims.evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2E, F and Figure 2—figure supplement 1D, E.

claims.claim: 100% of mad2 diplochromosome divisions exhibit lagging chromosomes or DNA bridges.
claims.source: Further, 100% of mad2 diplochromosome divisions exhibit lagging chromosomes, or DNA bridges (Figure 2—figure supplement 1F, Video 8), compared with 80% of divisions in HS>fzr cells.
claims.evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1F and Video 8.

claims.claim: Drosophila rectal papillar cells naturally undergo two fzr-dependent endocycles during the 2nd larval instar to generate octoploid cells.
claims.source: In earlier work we found Drosophila rectal papillar cells (hereafter: papillar cells) naturally undergo two fzr-dependent endocycles during the 2nd larval instar to generate octoploid cells and then divide, on average, two times during pupal development.
claims.evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work by the authors.

claims.claim: Papillar cells divide, on average, two times during pupal development.
claims.source: In earlier work we found Drosophila rectal papillar cells (hereafter: papillar cells) naturally undergo two fzr-dependent endocycles during the 2nd larval instar to generate octoploid cells and then divide, on average, two times during pupal development.
claims.evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work by the authors.

claims.claim: An intervening S-phase accompanies papillar polyploid divisions.
claims.source: An intervening S-phase accompanies these polyploid divisions, and cells at the papillar base undergo one additional S-phase after the final polyploid mitosis (Figure 3A; Fox et al., 2010; Schoenfelder et al., 2014).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citations to Fox et al., 2010 and Schoenfelder et al., 2014, and by Figure 3A.

claims.claim: Papillar chromosomes in octoploid cells are arranged in individual sister chromatid pairs at the first octoploid metaphase.
claims.source: Through careful re-examination of the first octoploid metaphase, we confirmed that papillar chromosomes in these octoploid cells are arranged in individual sister chromatid pairs (Figure 3B'' inset, C).
claims.evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3B'' inset and C.

claims.claim: Papillar cells re-enter mitosis from a G2-like state, as evidenced by expression of the G2/M regulator Cdc25/string just before the onset of pupal cell cycles.
claims.source: Papillar cells re-enter mitosis from a G2-like state, as evidenced by expression of the G2/M regulator Cdc25/string just before the onset of pupal cell cycles (Fox et al., 2010) (Figure 3—figure supplement 1A).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citation to Fox et al., 2010 and experimental data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1A.

claims.claim: At time points early in the first papillar mitosis, papillar chromosomes are polytene.
claims.source: At time points early in the first mitosis, we indeed find that papillar chromosomes are polytene (Figure 3B, Polytene).
claims.evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3B.

claims.claim: In papillar polytene cells, centromeres are able to separate into groups of homologs and further separate into individual sister chromatid pairs.
claims.source: However, unlike in cells with induced polyteny, the centromeres in papillar polytene cells are able to not only separate into groups of homologs, but to further separate into individual sister chromatid pairs (asterisks in Figure 3B and Figure 3—figure supplement 1B vs. Figure 1F, also see discussion).
claims.evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3B, Figure 3—figure supplement 1B, and Figure 1F.

claims.claim: In flies heterozygous for inversion-containing balancer chromosomes, papillar polytene structure is locally perturbed.
claims.source: In flies heterozygous for inversion-containing balancer chromosomes, papillar polytene structure is locally perturbed, likely due to the disruption of somatic homolog pairing (Figure 3—figure supplement 1B).
claims.evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1B and inference about the cause.

claims.claim: Neither the polytene nor the clumped configurations remain during the second papillar division.
claims.source: Neither the polytene nor the clumped configurations remain during the second division (Figure 3C,D), suggesting a specific chromosome structure is present early in the first division of papillar cells.
claims.evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3C and D.

claims.claim: By FISH, examples of both closely associated (polytene) and dispersed (separated/non-polytene) signals are found during the period of the first papillar mitosis.
claims.source: Similarly, by Fluorescent In Situ Hybridization (FISH) we find examples of both closely associated (polytene) and dispersed (separated/non-polytene) signals during the period of the first papillar mitosis (Figure 3—figure supplement 1C,C').
claims.evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1C, C'.

claims.claim: Using Premature Chromosome Compaction (PCC), clear polytene chromosomes are present in nearly every pre-mitotic papillar cell.
claims.source: Using this technique, we find that in pre-mitotic papillar tissue, clear polytene chromosomes are present in nearly every cell (Figure 3D Pre 1st Div, Figure 3—figure supplement 1B).
claims.evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3D and Figure 3—figure supplement 1B.

claims.claim: When papillar cells are enriched for metaphase by colcemid treatment, zero examples of polytene chromosomes are found.
claims.source: If we instead enrich for cells in metaphase of the first mitosis by treating with the spindle poison colcemid, we find zero examples where chromosomes are still polytene.
claims.evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3D.

claims.claim: Prior to the first papillar mitosis, the kinetochores from each homolog are closely associated into an average of 4.1 large foci.
claims.source: Prior to the first papillar mitosis, the kinetochores from each homolog are closely associated into an average of 4.1 large foci, close to the haploid number of distinct chromosomes (4 for females and 5 for males due to X/Y un-pairing, Figure 3E).
claims.evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3E.

claims.claim: During the first papillar division, large kinetochore foci disperse into many smaller foci prior to metaphase.
claims.source: As time progresses in the first division, it is possible to watch these large kinetochore foci disperse into many smaller foci prior to metaphase (Figure 3F, inset, Video 9).
claims.evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3F and Video 9.

claims.claim: Prior to the second papillar division, kinetochores are already separated into an average of 15.1 observably distinct foci per cell before entry into mitosis.
claims.source: In contrast, prior to the second division kinetochores are already separated into many more foci (an average of 15.1 observably distinct foci per cell) before entry into mitosis (Figure 3E).
claims.evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3E.

claims.claim: During the second papillar division, the number of resolvable kinetochore foci remains essentially constant.
claims.source: During the second division, the number of resolvable foci remains essentially constant (Figure 3G, Video 10).
claims.evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3G and Video 10.

claims.claim: Polytene chromosomes are visible when chromosomes first condense during the first papillar division and can be seen to disperse.
claims.source: Additionally, the histone marker reveals that polytene chromosomes are visible when chromosomes first condense and can then be seen to disperse during the first but not the second division (Figure 3F v. 3G, -18:00 min).
claims.evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3F and 3G.

claims.claim: Each clump of 4 or 5 pre-first division centromeres only contains a single chromosome type.
claims.source: We also confirmed that each clump of 4 or 5 pre-first division centromeres only contains a single chromosome type. To do so, we took advantage of the fact that dosage compensation in flies relies on upregulation of transcription on the male X chromosome via the Dosage Compensation Complex (Conrad and Akhtar, 2011). By live imaging papillar cells expressing the DCC complex protein MSL3 tagged with GFP, which localizes only to the male X-chromosome (Strukov et al., 2011), we find that indeed only a single Cenp-C-Tomato focus is MSL3-GFP positive prior to polytene dissociation (Figure 3—figure supplement 1D, Video 11).
claims.evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1D and Video 11, and by citations to Conrad and Akhtar, 2011 and Strukov et al., 2011.

claims.claim: Polytene chromosomes are present before polyploid mitosis in Culex pipiens.
claims.source: Inspired by classical reports (Berger, 1938; Grell, 1946; Holt, 1917), we found polytene chromosomes are present before polyploid mitosis in Culex, but are later apparent as individual chromosomes during mitosis (Figure 3—figure supplement 1E).
claims.evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1E and by citations to Berger, 1938; Grell, 1946; Holt, 1917.

claims.claim: First division mad2 papillar cells exhibit a substantial increase in DNA bridges.
claims.source: Because mad2 loss has no reported mitotic defects in Drosophila animals (Buffin et al., 2007), we were surprised to find that first division mad2 papillar cells exhibit a substantial increase in DNA bridges (Figure 4A,B, Video 13, Video 14).
claims.evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4A, B and Videos 13, 14, and by citation to Buffin et al., 2007.

claims.claim: Similar defects were not detected during papillar mitosis of animals null for mad1.
claims.source: We did not detect similar defects during papillar mitosis of animals null for mad1, another SAC component (Figure 4A,B, Video 15).
claims.evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4A, B and Video 15.

claims.claim: Colcemid treatment increases the mitotic index of wild type papillar cells.
claims.source: To first test if papillar cells employ the SAC wait-anaphase in response to polytene chromosomes, we treated animals with colcemid, a known SAC wait-anaphase trigger. This treatment increases the mitotic index of wild type papillar cells, whereas the mitotic index of mad2 null animals is unaffected (Figure 4C,D)
claims.evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4C and D.

claims.claim: The mitotic index of mad2 null papillar cells is unaffected by colcemid treatment.
claims.source: This treatment increases the mitotic index of wild type papillar cells, whereas the mitotic index of mad2 null animals is unaffected (Figure 4C,D)
claims.evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4C and D.

claims.claim: Metaphase is not any longer in the first papillar division than in the second papillar division.
claims.source: However we find that metaphase is not any longer in the first papillar division than in the second papillar division, while in contrast metaphase is almost twice as long in wing cells with diplochromosomes than in those that are polyploid but lack diplochromosomes (Figure 4E).
claims.evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4E.

claims.claim: Metaphase is almost twice as long in wing cells with diplochromosomes than in those that are polyploid but lack diplochromosomes.
claims.source: However we find that metaphase is not any longer in the first papillar division than in the second papillar division, while in contrast metaphase is almost twice as long in wing cells with diplochromosomes than in those that are polyploid but lack diplochromosomes (Figure 4E).
claims.evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4E.

claims.claim: SIRS occurs on schedule even in the presence of colcemid concentrations that are sufficient to eliminate a detectable spindle and inhibit anaphase.
claims.source: We find SIRS occurs on schedule even in the presence of colcemid concentrations that are sufficient to eliminate a detectable spindle and inhibit anaphase (Figure 4F,G, Video 16, Video 17).
claims.evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4F, G and Videos 16, 17.

claims.claim: Mad2 regulates NEBD-to-anaphase timing in papillar cells.
claims.source: Using an NEBD marker, we first confirmed that Mad2 regulates NEBD-to-anaphase timing and that mad2 cells spend significantly less time in mitosis than wild type cells (Figure 5A,B, Video 18, Video 19).
claims.evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5A, B and Videos 18, 19.

claims.claim: mad2 papillar cells spend significantly less time in mitosis than wild type cells.
claims.source: Using an NEBD marker, we first confirmed that Mad2 regulates NEBD-to-anaphase timing and that mad2 cells spend significantly less time in mitosis than wild type cells (Figure 5A,B, Video 18, Video 19).
claims.evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5A, B and Videos 18, 19.

claims.claim: Nuclear Envelope Breakdown and the onset of SIRS are synchronous in wild type papillar cells.
claims.source: We also find that Nuclear Envelope Breakdown and the onset of SIRS are synchronous in wild type cells and that SIRS generally continues until up to the onset of anaphase (Figure 5C).
claims.evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5C.

claims.claim: SIRS generally continues until up to the onset of anaphase in wild type papillar cells.
claims.source: We also find that Nuclear Envelope Breakdown and the onset of SIRS are synchronous in wild type cells and that SIRS generally continues until up to the onset of anaphase (Figure 5C).
claims.evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5C.

claims.claim: SIRS fails to complete before anaphase in mad2 animals, leading to a high variance of centromere intensity signal across the metaphase plate.
claims.source: From these measurements, we found that SIRS fails to complete before anaphase in mad2 animals, leading to a high variance of centromere intensity signal across the metaphase plate (reflecting failure of centromere dissociation/SIRS completion).
claims.evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5D and D'.

claims.claim: High variance of centromere signal disrupts the bilateral symmetry of the metaphase plate in mad2 cells that form DNA bridges.
claims.source: This high variance disrupts the bilateral symmetry of the metaphase plate in mad2 cells that form DNA bridges (Figure 5D').
claims.evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5D'.

claims.claim: Homolog-homolog dissociation is not unique to SIRS.
claims.source: Given that we observe the haploid number of chromosomes after both papillar (Figure 3B) and HS>fzr (Figure 1F) endocycles, it is clear that homologous chromosomes associate within both types of polytene chromosomes by somatic homolog pairing (Metz, 1916; Painter, 1934). Both mitotic papillar and HS>fzr polytenes exhibit un-paired homologs before dividing (Figure 3B'', Figure 1F'), and this process appears to initiate at centromeres (Figure 1F, Figure 3B, asterisks, most obvious for the acrocentric X chromosome). Thus, homolog-homolog dissociation is not unique to SIRS.
claims.evidence: This is based on inference from experimental data shown in Figures 1F, 3B, and 3B'', and citations to Metz, 1916 and Painter, 1934.

claims.claim: In SIRS-capable (e.g. papillar) cells, only the product of the single most recent round of replication (recent sisters) remain attached at metaphase.
claims.source: Importantly, the arrangement of chromatid pairs at metaphase differs between cells that do or do not undergo SIRS. In SIRS-capable (e.g. papillar) cells, only the product of the single most recent round of replication (recent sisters, see nomenclature) remain attached at metaphase whereas the products of previous rounds of replication are no longer attached.
claims.evidence: This is based on inference from experimental observations of chromosome structure.

claims.claim: In SIRS-incapable (e.g. HS>fzr) cells, all sister chromatids remain attached at metaphase.
claims.source: In contrast, in SIRS-incapable (e.g. HS>fzr) cells, all sister chromatids remain attached.
claims.evidence: This is based on inference from experimental observations of diplochromosome structure.

claims.claim: The key difference between SIRS-capable and SIRS-incapable cells is the ability to separate into sister chromatid pairs before metaphase.
claims.source: Taken together, we conclude the key difference between SIRS-capable (e.g. papillar) and SIRS-incapable (e.g, HS>fzr) cells is the ability to separate into sister chromatid pairs before metaphase (Figure 5E).
claims.evidence: This is a conclusion based on inference from multiple experimental observations.

claims.claim: Chromosome dispersal in polyploid Drosophila ovarian nurse cells represents an incomplete version of SIRS.
claims.source: Based on our results, we also suggest that chromosome dispersal in polyploid Drosophila ovarian nurse cells represents an incomplete version of SIRS (Dej and Spradling, 1999), especially given that these chromosomes can further separate if mitotic cyclins are experimentally elevated (Reed and Orr-Weaver, 1997).
claims.evidence: This is a suggestion based on inference from the current results and citations to Dej and Spradling, 1999 and Reed and Orr-Weaver, 1997.

claims.claim: Whole genome duplication is common (~37%) in human tumors.
claims.source: Whole genome duplication is common (~37%) in human tumors (Zack et al., 2013).
claims.evidence: This is supported by a citation to Zack et al., 2013.

results.result: Heat shock-induced fzr overexpression converts G2 cells to G1 by eliminating mitotic cyclins, leading to genome reduplication and formation of tetraploid cells with polytene chromosomes that progress to diplochromosomes at metaphase.
results.evaluation: Claims C44-C51 collectively demonstrate that HS>fzr induces endocycles by converting G2 to G1 (C45-C48), resulting in tetraploidy (C49) with polytene chromosomes (C50) that become diplochromosomes at metaphase (C51). The experimental evidence from FUCCI markers, PH3 staining, and karyotype analysis provides strong support for this experimental system.

results.result: Diplochromosomes cause high rates of mitotic errors (80% with lagging chromosomes or DNA bridges) through 3:1 segregation, but these errors are primarily due to diplochromosomes rather than tetraploidy itself, and aneuploid cells continue dividing for at least 5 days.
results.evaluation: Claims C52-C58 demonstrate that diplochromosomes cause frequent mitotic errors (C54, C55) that are specific to diplochromosomes rather than tetraploidy (C56), with centrosome amplification not being a major contributor (C57). Live imaging and karyotype data provide strong quantitative support, and the continued division of aneuploid cells (C58) is well-documented.

results.result: Organism survival is only subtly affected at low levels of tetraploidy (23%) but decreases in a dose-dependent manner with increased tetraploidy.
results.evaluation: Claims C59-C60 show a clear dose-response relationship between tetraploidy levels and survival, supported by quantitative data in Figure 2A. The experimental design appropriately varies heat shock duration to modulate tetraploidy levels.

results.result: Diplochromosomes trigger a Mad2-dependent spindle assembly checkpoint that extends metaphase duration, with BubR1 localizing asymmetrically to kinetochores suggesting attachment difficulties.
results.evaluation: Claims C61-C64 demonstrate SAC activation by diplochromosomes through extended metaphase (C61), Mad2-dependence (C62), and BubR1 localization patterns (C63-C64). Live imaging with quantitative timing measurements and BubR1-GFP localization provide strong mechanistic evidence for checkpoint activation.

results.result: Loss of Mad2 in HS>fzr animals causes severe survival defects (15.4% survival), tissue malformations, increased apoptosis, and 100% mitotic error rates, demonstrating that the Mad2-dependent anaphase delay is essential for survival after genome reduplication.
results.evaluation: Claims C65-C69 establish the critical role of Mad2 in responding to diplochromosomes. While mad2 alone is viable (C65), combining it with HS>fzr causes dramatic survival defects (C66), tissue abnormalities (C67), increased apoptosis (C68), and complete mitotic failure (C69). The data strongly support Mad2's protective role.

results.result: Drosophila papillar cells naturally undergo two endocycles to reach 8N, then divide twice during pupal development, with chromosomes arranged as individual sister chromatid pairs at metaphase despite being polytene early in the first mitosis.
results.evaluation: Claims C70-C76 describe the natural papillar cell cycle program, supported by prior publications (C70-C72, C74) and new observations showing polytene chromosomes early in mitosis (C75) that separate into sister pairs (C73, C76). The combination of prior work and new cytological data provides strong support.

results.result: SIRS (Separation Into Recent Sisters) is a process specific to the first papillar division where polytene chromosomes present in nearly all pre-mitotic cells (by PCC) completely separate into sister pairs before metaphase, as demonstrated by kinetochore dispersal from ~4 to ~15 foci and elimination of polytene chromosomes by colcemid-enriched metaphase.
results.evaluation: Claims C77-C87 provide comprehensive evidence for SIRS through multiple complementary approaches: PCC showing pre-mitotic polyteny (C80), colcemid showing metaphase separation (C81), quantitative kinetochore counting (C82-C85), live imaging (C83, C86), and MSL3-GFP confirming single chromosome types per focus (C87). The convergent evidence strongly supports SIRS as a distinct process.

results.result: Polytene chromosomes are present before polyploid mitosis in Culex pipiens mosquitoes, suggesting SIRS may be conserved.
results.evaluation: Claim C88 is supported by experimental data in Figure 3—figure supplement 1E and citations to classical literature. However, the evidence is more limited than for Drosophila papillar cells, showing only that polytene chromosomes exist pre-mitotically in Culex.

results.result: Mad2, but not Mad1, is required for efficient SIRS, as mad2 mutants show increased DNA bridges during the first papillar division, yet papillar cells retain a functional SAC response to colcemid.
results.evaluation: Claims C89-C92 demonstrate a Mad1-independent role for Mad2 in SIRS. The increased DNA bridges in mad2 (C89) but not mad1 (C90), combined with intact colcemid response in wild-type but not mad2 (C91-C92), support a dual role for Mad2. The genetic dissection is well-controlled.

results.result: SIRS does not trigger a SAC-mediated anaphase delay, as metaphase length is equal between first and second papillar divisions, and SIRS proceeds normally in the presence of colcemid that eliminates the spindle.
results.evaluation: Claims C93-C95 demonstrate that SIRS is independent of SAC wait-anaphase signaling through timing measurements (C93-C94) and colcemid experiments showing spindle-independent SIRS (C95). The comparison between papillar and wing cells (C94) provides an internal control showing the system can detect SAC activation.

results.result: Mad2 regulates NEBD-to-anaphase timing in papillar cells, with mad2 mutants showing shortened mitosis (14 vs 17 minutes), and SIRS normally occurring synchronously with NEBD and continuing until anaphase. In mad2 mutants, incomplete SIRS causes high variance in centromere signals and asymmetric metaphase plates in cells that form DNA bridges.
results.evaluation: Claims C96-C101 establish Mad2's role in mitotic timing during SIRS through quantitative live imaging with NEBD markers (C96-C99) and image analysis of centromere distributions (C100-C101). The correlation between incomplete SIRS, asymmetric metaphase plates, and DNA bridge formation provides strong mechanistic insight.

results.result: The key mechanistic difference between SIRS-capable and SIRS-incapable cells is the ability to separate polytene chromosomes into recent sister pairs before metaphase, with homolog dissociation occurring in both cell types but sister chromatid separation being unique to SIRS.
results.evaluation: Claims C102-C105 synthesize observations from both experimental systems to identify the critical distinction. The inference is well-supported by comparative analysis of chromosome structures in papillar vs HS>fzr cells, though the molecular mechanism enabling this difference remains to be determined.

results.result: When polytene chromosomes persist to metaphase, a Mad2-dependent anaphase delay substantially reduces (but does not eliminate) apoptosis, tissue malformation, and organismal death, despite not fully preventing mitotic errors and aneuploidy.
results.evaluation: Claims C7, C37-C39 describe the first major response to reduplicated chromosomes. The protective but incomplete nature of the SAC response is well-supported by survival data (C39), apoptosis measurements (C39), and error rate quantification (C38). The data clearly show Mad2's beneficial role despite imperfect error correction.

results.result: SIRS is a spindle-independent mechanism that eliminates polyteny before anaphase without triggering a Mad2-dependent anaphase delay, but requires Mad2's control of mitotic timing to allow sufficient time for completion.
results.evaluation: Claims C8, C40-C43 describe the second major response to reduplicated chromosomes. The spindle-independence (C40), complete elimination of polyteny (C41), lack of anaphase delay (C42), and requirement for Mad2 timing function (C43) are all well-supported by experimental data including colcemid experiments and mad2 mutant analysis.

results.result: Both reduplication responses (anaphase delay for metaphase polytenes and SIRS) require Mad2, but through distinct mechanisms: anaphase delay for diplochromosomes versus control of overall mitotic timing for efficient SIRS.
results.evaluation: Claims C9-C11 represent the central unifying conclusion of the paper. The requirement for Mad2 in both contexts (C9) through different mechanisms (C10-C11) is strongly supported by the genetic and live imaging experiments throughout the manuscript. This represents a novel insight into Mad2 function.

results.result: Polytene chromosomes formed by genome reduplication contain multiple layers of physical connections (cohesins, topological entanglements, homolog pairing) and are considered mechanically problematic for mitosis, causing chromosome mis-segregation.
results.evaluation: Claims C1-C3, C12-C22 provide background on normal chromosome behavior and polytene chromosome structure. These are well-established facts supported by extensive prior literature (multiple citations provided). The claims accurately represent current knowledge about polytene chromosome organization and its challenges for mitosis.

results.result: Chromosome reduplication and polytene chromosomes occur in diverse contexts including development, disease (tumors, abortions, muscular dystrophy), and following chemotherapy or disruption of mitotic processes, across many species including humans.
results.evaluation: Claims C4-C6, C23-C31 establish the biological and medical relevance of the study through extensive citations to prior literature. These background claims are well-supported by the cited references and establish the importance of understanding cellular responses to polyteny.

results.result: Drosophila papillar cells are built by mitosis of endocycled cells, yet polytene chromosomes were never observed at metaphase in hundreds of cells, and prior studies suggest polyteny can be partially undone without anaphase.
results.evaluation: Claims C32-C34 establish the rationale for studying papillar cells as a model system. The claims are supported by prior publications from the authors' lab (C32-C33) and other studies (C34), providing the foundation for investigating how papillar cells avoid metaphase polyteny.

results.result: Mad2 inhibits the Anaphase Promoting Complex to both delay anaphase in response to unattached/tensionless kinetochores and regulate overall mitotic timing from NEBD to anaphase onset.
results.evaluation: Claims C35-C36 describe established Mad2 functions based on prior literature (London and Biggins, 2014; Musacchio, 2015). These are accurate representations of known Mad2 biology that provide context for the novel findings about Mad2's dual roles in responding to polyteny.

results.result: Chromosome dispersal in polyploid Drosophila ovarian nurse cells may represent an incomplete version of SIRS.
results.evaluation: Claim C106 is explicitly presented as a suggestion/speculation based on inference from the current results and prior work. While the hypothesis is reasonable given that nurse cell chromosomes can further separate with elevated mitotic cyclins, this remains untested and speculative. Additional experiments would be needed to confirm this interpretation.

results.result: Whole genome duplication is common (~37%) in human tumors.
results.evaluation: Claim C108 is a factual statement supported by citation to Zack et al., 2013. This provides important context for the medical relevance of the findings but is not a result of the current study.
